issue: Source has the passive "the utility and necessity of a federal judicature have been clearly pointed out"; candidate "I made clear the usefulness and necessity" adds a claim of personal authorship of earlier numbers that the source does not make.
replacement: In setting out the defects of the existing Confederation, the usefulness and necessity of a federal judiciary were clearly pointed out. I need not review the considerations urged there, because no one disputes that the institution is proper in principle. The only questions raised concern how it is to be constituted and how far its authority is to extend. Our observations will therefore be confined to those two points.

issue: Source "this consideration will afford a strong argument for the permanent tenure of judicial offices, since nothing will contribute so much as this to that independent spirit": candidate splits into two sentences and drops the connective "since" (STYLE-NOTE: keep logical connectives) and the comparison "as this".
replacement: If, then, the courts of justice are to be considered the bulwarks of a limited Constitution against legislative encroachments, this strongly supports permanent tenure for judicial offices, since nothing will contribute so much as that tenure to the independent spirit in the judges which is essential to the faithful performance of so arduous a duty.

issue: Source "must ultimately depend upon the aid of the executive arm": candidate drops "the aid of".
replacement: Anyone who carefully considers the different departments of power must see that in a government where they are kept separate from one another, the judiciary, by the nature of its functions, will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution, because it will be the least able to annoy or injure them. The Executive not only dispenses the honors but holds the sword of the community. The legislature not only controls the purse but prescribes the rules by which the duties and rights of every citizen are to be regulated. The judiciary, by contrast, has no influence over either the sword or the purse; it has no direction of the strength or of the wealth of the society, and can take no active resolution whatever. It may truly be said to have neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment; and in the end it must depend on the aid of the executive arm even for the effectiveness of its judgments.

issue: Source "peculiarly essential" rendered "above all", which adds a ranking ("most important") instead of "especially".
replacement: The complete independence of the courts of justice is especially essential in a limited Constitution. By a limited Constitution I mean one that sets out certain specific exceptions to the legislative authority; for instance, that the legislature may pass no bills of attainder and no ex post facto laws, and so on. In practice, such limitations can be kept only through courts of justice, whose duty it must be to declare all acts contrary to the manifest tenor of the Constitution void. Without this, every reservation of particular rights or privileges would come to nothing.

issue: Source "might in half a century become penurious and inadequate": "penurious" here means meager, scanty. Candidate "miserly" means stingy and is the wrong sense for a salary.
replacement: All things considered, this is the best provision that could have been devised. It is easy to understand that fluctuations in the value of money and in the state of society made it inadmissible to fix a rate of compensation in the Constitution. What might be extravagant today might in half a century become meager and inadequate. It was therefore necessary to leave it to the discretion of the legislature to vary the provisions as circumstances vary, yet under such restrictions as to put it out of that body's power to make any individual's condition worse. A man may then be sure of the ground he stands on, and can never be deterred from his duty by fear of being placed in a less favorable situation. The clause I have quoted combines both advantages. The salaries of judicial officers may be altered from time to time as occasion requires, but never so as to reduce the allowance with which any particular judge comes into office, as far as he is concerned. It will be noticed that the Convention made a difference between the compensation of the President and that of the judges. The President's can be neither increased nor diminished; the judges' can only not be diminished. This probably arose from the difference in the length of the two offices. Since the President is to be elected for no more than four years, it can rarely happen that a salary adequate at the beginning of that period will fail to remain so to its end. But the judges, if they behave properly, will be secure in their places for life. It may well happen, especially in the early stages of the government, that a stipend quite sufficient when they are first appointed would become too small as their service goes on.

issue: Source "The latter ... and, I presume, will be most agreeable to the States": subject is the latter (the courts' power). Candidate "and, I presume, it will be more agreeable" has an ambiguous "it" that reads as the Convention.
replacement: The first point rests on this obvious consideration: there ought always to be a constitutional method of giving effect to constitutional provisions. What, for instance, would restrictions on the authority of the State legislatures be worth without some constitutional means of enforcing them? Under the plan of the Convention the States are forbidden to do a variety of things, some of which are incompatible with the interests of the Union and others with the principles of good government. Imposing duties on imported articles and issuing paper money are examples of each kind. No sensible man will believe that such prohibitions would be scrupulously respected unless the government had some effective power to restrain or correct violations of them. This power must be either a direct negative on the State laws, or an authority in the federal courts to overrule those that were in manifest contravention of the articles of Union. I can imagine no third course. The Convention appears to have thought the latter preferable to the former, and, I presume, the latter will be more agreeable to the States.

issue: Source "in order to the inviolable maintenance of that equality ... the national judiciary ought to preside" is a means-to-end claim. Candidate "Only so can the equality ... be inviolably maintained" asserts exclusivity ("only") that the source does not state.
replacement: It may be considered the basis of the Union that "the citizens of each State shall be entitled to all the privileges and immunities of citizens of the several States." And if it is a sound principle that every government ought to have the means of executing its own provisions by its own authority, it follows that, in order to maintain inviolably the equality of privileges and immunities to which the citizens of the Union will be entitled, the national judiciary ought to preside in all cases in which one State or its citizens are opposed to another State or its citizens. To secure the full effect of so fundamental a provision against all evasion and subterfuge, its interpretation must be committed to that court which, having no local attachments, is likely to be impartial between the different States and their citizens, and which, owing its official existence to the Union, will never be likely to feel any bias unfavorable to the principles on which the Union is founded.

issue: Source "such regulations as will be calculated to obviate or remove these inconveniences" (aimed at, not guaranteed). Candidate "as will remove those problems" drops "calculated to obviate or" and strengthens the claim to certainty.
replacement: This review of the particular powers of the federal judiciary, as marked out in the Constitution, shows that they all conform to the principles that ought to have governed the structure of that department, and that were necessary to the perfection of the system. If some particular problems should appear to be connected with including any of them in the plan, we should remember that the national legislature will have ample authority to make such exceptions, and to prescribe such regulations, as are calculated to prevent or remove those problems. A well-informed mind can never regard the possibility of particular harms as a solid objection to a general principle that is meant to avoid general harms and to obtain general advantages.
